item.title: SCP-5127-J ( A joke SCP) Any thoughts?: SCP-5127-J ( A joke SCP) Any thoughts?
item.content:encoded:
[[include component:image-block | name=https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/The-Office-Michael-Scott-cringe-square.jpg| caption= Michael Scott | width=WIDTH-GOES-HERE]]

Item #: SCP-5127-J

Object Class: Euclid

Special Containment Procedures: SCP-5127-J is to be kept inside Steve Carell's mansion. There it has a room that the foundation has made into a look-alike Michael Scott's office. To Keep SCP-5127-J busy, It has a number of desk toys that It can interact and play with. Including a Train whistle, a small slinky, a rubric's cube and silly putty. It also can be kept busy with a phone with recorded voices.

Description: SCP-5127-J is a translucent ghost version of Michael Gary Scott, the branch manager of Dunder Mifflin Scranton SCP-5127-J first appeared when Steve Carell finished The Office in 2011. Before the foundation knew anything about SCP-5127-J, It was roaming Steve Carell's mansion. After Steve Carrel said anything, SCP-5127-J responded with "That's what she said" which made anything Steve said seem wrong. It happened so frequently, Steve Carrel began to lose money from low self esteem and stress. The foundation kept his losses under wraps as they would eventually ruin his career. He wrote letters to the producers and begged them to let him back on to the show. Eventually in the last episode, They let him back in. For a while during the recording, SCP-5127-J was silent. But when they aired the episode, SCP-5127-J came back. The first instance after the show was when Steve was cleaning up after the family meal and he said," I'm going to put this back." and SCP-5127-J responded," That's what she said." Recently the foundation has recorded 600,000 USD that Steve Carrel has lost to SCP-5127-J.

item.title: Lost in the Fog / Temporal SCP: Re: Lost in the Fog / Temporal SCP
item.content:encoded:
Responding to IRC request

"People assume that time is a strict progression of cause to affect, but actually, from a non-linier, non subjective point of view it is more like a big ball of wibbily wobbly timey wimey…stuff.

-The Tenth Doctor

I should let you know that I'm no pro in clincal tone, but my dialogue is definitely better, so I'll absolutely be of more help there.

Without further ado…

+Let us start the crit!
-Let's do it!

A Foundation meteorological team is to be stationed on Site-287 at all times,

I feel like 'in' or 'at' would work better than 'on' for 'stationed on Site-287.'

which is to receive additional staffing during the Spring and Fall, as there is an increased risk of manifestations during this period.

Probably just a personal thing, but I'd use 'Autumn' over 'Fall.'
And change 'this period' to 'these periods'.

All efforts should be oriented toward predicting precise dates and times when SCP-XXXX will appear.

This line reads a bit strangely. We can change it to, 'All efforts should be focused towards predicting the precise times for SCP-XXXX appearances.'

Note: the seasons (like Spring and Fall) aren't proper nouns, so they don't need to be capitalized.

Extensive research has shown that all victims had been traveling during clear skies and when the difference in air temperature and dew point was less than 2.5 °C (4.5 °F), conditions favorable for the formation of fog.

The first and second half of this feel oddly disjointed.

I think you can separate the 'clear skies' bit and the 'conditions favorable for the formation of fog' bit.

Clinical tone pretty good so far. I'm impressed.

I'm about to hit the video logs. Let's take a closer look, shall we?

Containment Log

Richardson: Yes sir.

Comma after 'yes'.

Carter: You know, how come we're the only ones out here hunting this thing? There are other MTFs better equipped to handle stuff like this.

Richardson: What's the matter, Carter? You afraid of a little Jurassic Park?

I'm personally not a fan of this because I can't imagine highly trained MTF agents being this unprofessional, going as far as to complain on the job. Also, I doubt the Foundation would send the wrong MTF into this anomaly. I do remember what the plot twist was, though, so I'll bite for the time being.

Williams: Grow up, Richardson.

Honestly, I kind of agree. Granted, this might just be a personal thing and only a personal thing, but I'm still not fond of this unprofessional dialogue. It's too…cheesy, I guess. For something as serious as a time-based anomaly releasing pre-historic stuff into modern times.

He notices something laying on the ground.

lying* on the ground.
I actually had to google this, so I'll just copy-paste the reason why it's lying and I'll also bold it out.

The verb ‘laying’ means ‘putting something somewhere’. The verb ‘lying’ means ‘telling falsehoods’ or ‘resting’ or ‘reclining’.

Miller stares into the lens and gives a cocky grin before turning in the direction of the truck.

This almost makes me forgive the unprofessional feel, just because of how Persona 5 this feels.

Closing Statement: The camera was successfully handed over to Foundation personnel and the prehistoric creature, nicknamed "Petrie", was transported to Site-135 for study.

MTF agents making jokes and wisecracks on the field, while not my cup of tea, at least could work. I know for sure that official Foundation documentation wouldn't recognize nicknames.

Log 1:

The camera has a hard time auto-adjusting as the fog swirls around the team.

Let's try, 'The camera struggles to auto-adjust as the fog swirls around the team.'

Williams: Please step out of the veh—

I think you should clarify that the vehicle actually stopped. I kinda assumed that it kept moving.

Richardson: Or when he disappeared to.

Carter: Shut up, Richardson.

Richardson: What? I'm just being specific.

Why do they bicker like high school classmates?

"Or when he disappeared to" makes me think of Scooby Doo for some reason. I have no idea why.

Miller: Uh, hi. What's your name?

I get the impression that this MTF is more like bumbling, socially awkward young adults rather than trained anomaly-handling Foundation personnel.

Carter: Shit, he’s serious about killing this guy.

Why does this man sound so oblivious to the fact that these opposing-forces civil war era soldiers are trying to kill each other?

I want to ask why the MTF didn't just leave after command said so and stayed behind to watch two civil war era soldiers fistfight, but then again, I can excuse this…seeing actual civil war era soldiers appearing before me would definitely hook my attention as well.

Log 2:

Carter: The mission?

Why wouldn't this person know the mission? I'd like to assume mission briefings are a thing in the Foundationverse, headcanon or not.

Now they're starting to sound more like MTF soldiers stuck in a temporal anomaly and not like idiotic high school students.

Brooks walks to the side of the road and unzips his pants. He conducts his business.

I want to comment on why this is mentioned and not just written as, 'Brooks steps off to the side for a moment,' but I'm not sure if that's even necessary. Ignore this part for now.

Apologies, by the way, the unprofessional dialogue is making me increasingly nitpicky.

Brooks: Uh… someone there?

I feel like a trained MTF soldier would stay quiet to try to gauge any potential, hidden threats.

Command: (pauses) Agent Miller, we have no one of that name or designation within our records.

Now things are picking up. I the professional feel of this part. Imo, this is how the dialogue should have been from the start.

But I can see what you were going for. I just don't like the amount of, 'uh, um, what?' and 'uh, okay, um' that are present left and right.

The camera pans upward to see a Tyrannosaurus Rex coming out of the trees and biting down on Brooks, lifting his body.

My inner Jurassic Park fanboyed at this. I approve.

Log 3:

The camera activates, flickers to view.

Remove comma, put 'and' between 'activates' and 'flickers'

The camera falls off the pile of sticks. Miller can be heard cursing at it before it shuts off.

I liked this part because of how solid it felt when I read it. That said, the dialogue here is okay. He's speaking more proper now, which is to be expected, considering how fucked he is here, no time to be making jokes. I don't feel the emotion here, though. I didn't really get to know his fellow soldiers aside from the unprofessional (sorry I keep tossing this word around left and right) banter and excessive, 'uh, um, what do I—' that I kept reading.

Story-wise, it works. Emotion-wise, I felt nothing too deep or personal. Intrigue? Yes. Investment into the characters? No.

Log 4:

Miller: (breathing heavily) So I've been thinking. SCP-XXXX is different than we thought. Maybe the fog exists in multiple points in time. Like a hub. That's why we kept running into all those people back there.

Or it's more like a big ball of wibbly wobbly, timey wimey stuff?
Couldn't resist ^_^

Also, this tidbit is intriguing.

Miller: You know, I don't have a lot of regrets in life, come to think of it. I had a great childhood, married a beautiful woman, had two precious girls. And then, for some reason, I got this job. I thought, oh hey, there's something I can get behind. A job that really makes a difference, you know? Containing threats and capturing dangerous entities. And not for fame or fortune either, since no one outside the Foundation knows about us. Or that we're out here, you know, protecting them. But you know what? That's fine. At least I used to go home every day proud that I was making the world a better place for my family.

I liked this part and felt something from it, even though 'narrate-monologues about my life choices in the face of imminent death' is kind of, if not overdone (I actually have no idea if it is), can still be considered a trope, afaik. Still, I liked this part. Thinking about loved ones in the face of danger always works.

This part also vaguely reminds me of SCP-3001. Extremely vaguely. As in, 'dude gets stuck in fuck-my-life-land and hates his life and reminisces on loved one/lover.'

I think you get the point.

There was a draft I read not too long ago where I remarked on why the camera-man kept repeatedly recording themselves doing things when it would have been more convenient to just…not do so, in universe, and it read like the camera was on just for the sake of showing story.

Here? In this draft? It sort of feels like that, but being alone in the face of temporal, foggy madness, having something mundane like this can help keep one at least somewhat sane. So I give it a pass here.

Miller: Yeah I guess that was too much to hope for.

Comma after 'Yeah'.

Miller: Poor thing. Looks like it's been through a lot. I think it's still recording.

Satisfying ending, despite every issue I stated earlier.

+Final thoughts.
-Yeet!

All in all, an iffy execution at the moment. I found the events themselves interesting as well as what was happening interesting, but the dialogue peaked at pretty acceptable and dipped to cringey and awkward and unprofessional. I can get behind wisecracking teammates on the field, but like, acting like immature, awkward constantly confused high school students pulled me out of the otherwise interesting adventure and bogged down the Containment Log as well as Logs 1 and 2.

I found no significant clinical tone issues, but I'm still not a pro in that field, so definitely run that by someone who is.

I can still see flashes of brilliance in this draft and I definitely look forward to the final product.

Either way, I hope I wasn't too harsh and I hope you find this helpful. I bid you the best of luck and wish you a fruitful journey on your first SCP!

As per the Draft Forum Policies, new authors are to get their concepts reviewed and greenlighted by two experienced reviewers on the Idea Critique Forums before posting on the Draft Critique Forums.

During the conceptualization stage, reviewers can give assistance in developing an idea before a draft is written. They can also assist in letting you know if something similar exists on the site already, or inform you of various clichés/pitfalls to be cautious of. These elements are more effectively addressed earlier in the writing process.

If you would like to request a draft review without greenlights, you can use the IRC Chatrooms to solicit critique.

If you have already received the requisite greenlights, please note the thread in which you received them, or the users whom provided them.

item.title: SCP Draft: Extra-Dimensional Vacuum Cleaner: Re: SCP Draft: Extra-Dimensional Vacuum Cleaner
item.content:encoded:
Hello! To start off, I am not on the butterfly roster so take this with grain of salt.

Crit
Hide crit

Upon opening your article I immediately noticed some formatting issues. "Item #:" should be bolded, it looks like you forgot to put the closing asterisks. The "Item #:" field should only contain the designation number, not the actual name of your SCP.

For your containment procedures, you don't need to state things that are already the "normal thing to do". Specifically:

The closet is to be locked at all times unless SCP-XXXX is currently undergoing testing

This is already implied. You can reword this to "Access to SCP-XXXX is strictly limited to testing."

After running SCP-XXXX for exactly 15 minutes, SCP-XXXX must be shut off immediately, and must not be interacted with for 35 minutes after use.

This is worded non-clinically and sounds out of place as a result. Additionally, it leaves the question of "what do we do if it's left on for longer?". Try "Should SCP-XXXX remain in an active state for longer than 15 minutes […]".

After removing and opening the storage compartment of SCP-XXXX, Class A personnel and higher may remove the contents of the bag. Failure to comply with these guidelines will lead to swift termination.

Again, clinical tone. Try "Removal of SCP-XXXX's storage compartment and its contents is restricted to assigned personnel with Class A clearance."

If SCP-XXXX is interacted with too quickly between uses, SCP-XXXX will teleport the violator to an unknown dimension, presumably the origin of the items SCP-XXXX produces.

This is not a containment procedure and does not belong here. Now onto the description:

SCP-XXXX resembles a pre-owned Oreck Vacuum Cleaner, about 1 meter high when assembled

Does the object resemble a vacuum cleaner, or is it a vacuum cleaner? If it's a man who shape-shifted into a vacuum, then it would "resemble" one. If it's a vacuum with anomalous powers, however, it's still a vacuum. Also, you don't need to state the height of the object unless it's significant to its anomalous properties.

When plugged into a standard American power outlet, SCP-XXXX will begin to emit a loud suction sound, comparable to any other vacuum.

You don't need to state this. In other words, you've said "When it's plugged in, the vacuum will make sounds like a vacuum." Remove it.

When used, SCP-XXXX will not remove any dirt, grime or debris from the ground, but will seem to pull from other dimensions.

Again, the wording here is weird. "When used" how? "will seem to pull" what "from other dimensions"? Assuming you meant matter, how has the Foundation confirmed this is where it originates from. How do they know the object is not manifesting matter instead? How do they know the matter is from another dimension instead of just a distant location in this one?

Previous testing's of SCP-XXXX have yielded:

This sentence is worded poorly. "Testing with SCP-XXXX has provided inconsistent results." would work better. I would also consider expanding on the narrative here since there really isn't one elsewhere. If the vacuum "steals" matter from other locations, what are the consequences in those locations?

Addendum:

I'll admit that I skimmed through this as it just didn't seem that interesting. The addendum adds nothing we didn't already know and only raises more questions than it answers.

In short, I think the basic idea of the object is interesting and can go somewhere. The draft, in the current state it's in now, needs a lot of revision. I think you need to focus on developed a central narrative / story for this because as it stands currently, it's just an anomalous item.

item.title: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly: Re: SCP-something: Man unable to communicate properly
item.content:encoded:
Thanks for the advice! The food for thought was very nutritious.
I completely agree that there were some unnecessary redactions, and I've removed the extraneous ones.
I never meant to give the impression that the Foundation was hostile towards SCPxx, only that Dr Adam Pink was. I've made a few adjustments to make that point clearer.
As for the ending, I'll agree that there are several rather unconnected threads, and that there is no clear conclusion to the story. However (and I may be blaspheming with this statement), is that such a bad thing? My goal with the article is for the reader to feel drawn into the mystery, and to feel a level of compassion for the SCP. I think most of the article does a reasonable job of fostering that. The sideline with the missing husband, in my opinion, is reasonably unsettling if nothing else.
I should also mention that one of my goals for the article was to write it in such a way that the SCP might not be anomalous at all.
In any case, I don't doubt that I'll be making adjustments to the article for a while yet. Thank you for looking at it!

item.title: The thrilling world of Foundation bureaucracy: Re: The thrilling world of Foundation bureaucracy
item.content:encoded:
Originally I was going for a less intensive, purposefully weak object that took a backseat to what an internal investigation within the foundation might look like, and how an organization with zero transparency might carry out, or fail to do that.

If you'd suffer a reference for a moment, I'd like to point toward SCP-5236, which deals with a similar investigative framework — difference being that the anomaly in question is a dead man, fractured into temporal bits by an anomalous drug. The idea invites provocation and easily spins into the story about the larger investigation.

Anyways. Best of luck!

item.title: An scp draft for a shower curtain (Need crits!): Re: An scp draft for a shower curtain (Need crits!)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Overall
[-] Overall

This suffers from a range of problems. I have highlighted a lot of examples of just, not good writing: I recommend grabbing something like LibreOffice Writer or Grammarly and running this through it to try and fix up a lot of the grammar.

Your ConProcs and Description are both big blocks of text that need broken up more. In particular, your ConProcs feel overly detailed and introduce a range of things that aren't referenced again (e.g. it being tied up, inspections, armed guards, etc), and it feels like it could be streamlined down to stuff that's either interesting (e.g. details of it replicating appendages) or a hook for later material.

The core problem with a lot of the rest is that the flow of information is just…not very good? You have a discovery section and two addendums that don't really add a tonne beyond vaguely referencing the core horror here; followed by a relatively bland re-telling of something horrifying which really feels like it needs to be like…something happening in real time, y'know?

This is rounded out with a note that spells out uh what feels like it should be everything but doesn't actually convey anything beyond what the discovery already implied and that it has extra magical powers that the foundation knows about…somehow. Iunno: this note feels excessively like having a character just stand there and go 'oh yes this thing is really dangerous super risky, if it got too big, it could destroy everything' instead of like…establishing that? By showing it?

If I am to be extremely real with this: in the current state I would downvote this and I would not expect it to survive. This is really going to need a lot of work to get into a serviceable state.

[-] Overall
[+] Line By Line
[-] Line By Line

Gonna note that I can miss stuff; flag things which are right as being wrong and indeed flag things which are deliberately wrong.
I'll likely use strikethrough to indicate stuff to remove and green text to indicate stuff to add.

SCP-XXXX shown and hung before containment.

I feel like 'SCP-XXXX before being contained.' would be clearer; really it's the 'shown and hung' that feels super awkward to me; and I'm trying to avoid having to handle that. Picking one of the two would likely work too.

SCP-XXXX resides in a compact box consisting of concrete

'resides' feels very passive; like it's just kinda in there for whatever reason; whereas something like 'is contained' sets up more of a feeling of it being a deliberate choice.

'consisting of' is weird here; it's technically correct I guess but something like 'made out of' or 'constructed from' would be clearer.

set on a table in a soundproof room in site-19.

why is it on a table? Also site names are capitalised (i.e. "Site-19").

Scp-XXXX is to be tied up with any sort of bonded material such as fiber or elastic rope when not in examination.

SCP is always capitalised; which is something you've not done a few times here.

What does 'tied up' mean here? Like, hung up like a shower curtain? Restrained as if it was alive? Why does it have to be done with a bonded material?

Research and inspection checks are to be made when SCP-XXXX has consumed enough matter to increase or exceed above its average size

This comes across a little weird because it feels like you should establish it has material to consume before mentioning it's consumed matter; or mention that it's not to be allowed to consume matter first.

or when recent developments and info have been made regarding SCP-XXXX.

'into SCP-XXXX' would likely feel less awkward than 'have been made regarding SCP-XXXX' here.

Only researchers with clearance level 3 or higher are allowed within the confinement of the anomaly’s cell.

During an inspection, standard earplugs, as well as protective equipment: such as class-A hazmat suits, must be worn during the process.

This is just, awkward. Consider: "During an inspection, protective equipment including earplugs and Class-A hazmat suits must be worn."

If SCP-XXXX is seen or noted replicating appendages, limbs; or any extremities that were once part of SCP-XXXX-A such as eyes, arms, veins, hair or legs.

You open this sentence with an 'If', follow it with a big list of conditions, and then end it without saying what happens if the conditions are true. I would probably trim this down a lot: appendages and limbs are roughly synonymous; and 'eyes' and 'veins' aren't extremities.

Consider: "If SCP-XXXX replicates appendages or any body parts that were once part of SCP-XXXX-A, then…"

With the addition of two armed guards to be stationed outside of the containment chamber until SCP-XXXX is starved enough were re-containment inside SCP-XXXX’s box is plausible.

This is a weird sentence fragment that feels like it's meant to be part of the previous sentence but was broken up cos it'd be super long if you didn't. Perhaps 'During the lockdown, two armed guards are to be….'

'plausible' would be better replaced with 'possible'

SCP-XXXX's extra exterminates will deteriorate over a period of time without the consistency of sustaining itself.

I believe you mean 'extremities' and not 'exterminates' here?

'without the consistency of sustaining itself' is not a phrase that I can parse. I believe something like "without the provision of matter to sustain it" would work better?

SCP-XXXX can manipulate and move these limbs seemingly with apparent ease. Scp-XXXX’s main goal seems to consist of blending in as seamlessly as possible with the former exception of any or all extra extremities that can break the illusion of Scp-XXXX’s disguise.

Both of these sentences would be better suited to the description.

SCP-XXXX is a 3 m x 1.5 m white shower curtain

On the one hand, this is a really big, weirdly proportioned shower curtain; on the other, it kinda feels like the size doesn't matter?

and bears signs of considerable use, molding, and age

I feel like 'considerable use' and 'age' are kinda…synonymous?

Subjects within a 10 m radius of SCP-XXXX that hear the whispers undergo a hypnotic and frenzied state.

This is the moment in the draft where my doubts go from 'this is a little janky but with some changes, it could work' to 'big concern that this is just not an interesting thing'.

The whispers feel like such a weird cliche and it's coupled with a) rage state b) compulsion effect that it just feels here like this is a bad coldpost. And it's a shame because the idea of the curtain absorbing people is great and this just feels entirely unnecessary.

Footnote 1: It is currently observed that animals such as: Domesticated dogs, cats, and even cases of un-domesticated wolves, deer, and bears are unaffected by SCP-XXXX’s anomaly’s effects. It is unknown if this applies to all types of animals including sets of particular species or just the ones listed.

This is wack. Just, really confusing list: I think you're wanting a semi-colon after wolves to separate 'and even undomesticated wolves' from 'deer and bears are unaffected' but really it doesn't feel like any of this detail is important or interesting.

While the appendage or limb that’s stuck is to be amputated immediately.

This is another one of those sentences that reads like it was meant to be part of the last sentence and then you just shoved a period into a random place to split it up so it wasn't too long.

'that's stuck' also feels really casual here; perhaps 'that is attached to SCP-XXXX is to be amputated…' would work better?

Salvaging as much as possible off of SCP-XXXX to avoid the further feeding and development of SCP-XXXX.

Yet another weird sentence that feels cut off the last sentence. I'm gonna stop highlighting this.

After a period of one (1) to three (3) days

The "one (1)" notation is only really done in cases where precision is really important (generally dispensing pharmaceuticals) and I would advise basically never doing it.

from contact (or died from natural causes) The following anomalies' effects will begin to take place.

random mid sentence capital

Rapidly succumbing to blood loss shortly after.

sentence fragment

will start to give off an unusual odor, consistent with the subject's last eaten meal. Or Inin rare caseswith ████.

This redaction sucks. Anyone who is cleared to know about this SCP needs to know what odours to expect here so they can make sure there's not a containment breach; and from an out-of-universe position, anything you put here is likely a lot more interesting than a box that says "*shrugs* iunno"

SCP-XXXX-A will become aggressive and irritable

why?

If enough human matter equivalent to SCP-XXXX’s current size and weight is consumed within a recorded one (1) to two (2) day period

'equivalent' feels janky here, maybe 'equal to' would be better?

When in this state, SCP-XXXX can enhance all senses which include: smell, hearing, vision, taste, and touch.

how do they know this?

SCP-XXXX seems to be able to manipulate and move these limbs around itself to better blend in and close distance between itself and its target.

'seems to'? It either has done this and can or hasn't done this and can't, it doesn't seem like there's much room for uncertainty.

Champagne Illinois on 7/27/2005 (Stated below).

I'm using this to say that a table for these addendums is a bad choice. I would probably label the first bit 'Discovery' and then having the rest as standalone headers in the style of "Description: words here"

Due to a three day period of silence designated from 7/27/2005 - 7/30/2005

'designated' is really weirdly shoved in here and can easily be cut.

225 reports of civilian deaths were filled by Champagne Illinois to the Foundation

do you mean 'filed'? Why is a town filing them to the Foundation like the Foundation is a secret organisation?

As an immediate response to this unusual jump and spike of numbers. The Foundation took interest and shut out every entrance into this town, making it a priority that no one enters or leaves the surrounding area.

yet another awkward sentence break, though this time you leave the start awkward, not the end.

I am going to stop for real this time: your writing is littered with poor sentence structure like this.

(Commander Linwood proceeds to slam his hands on the table, standing up in anger.)

I'd use italics (//italicised text// gives italicised text) to make these feel more distinct from the speech.

Stuff like this could be done between dialogue lines too for more emphasis:

Dr. Connor: Do you know why the wouldn't stop screaming, commander?

(Commanded Linwood proceeds to slam his hands on the table and stand up in anger.)

MTF Epsilon-6 commander Linwood: I don’t fucking know why. I’m still hear aren't I!? If I stuck around trying to help and console my men, I wouldn’t be alive, talking to you.

I'd also shorten Linwood's title here to just e.g. Linwood or Cmdr Linwood

Closing Remarks from doctor conner:

Both 'doctor' and 'conner' should be capitalised here.

SCP-XXXX has shown complete sentience beyond previous thought

'previously'? this is hard to parse

it posses several other anomalies effects that are not able to be used because it remains here on earth

'anomalous'

[-] Line By Line

item.content:encoded:
Author, per the Draft Forum's new policy: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-10629348/new-draft-forum-policies authors who have not yet posted a successful mainsite article are now required to get their basic concept(s) greenlighted by two experienced reviewers in the Ideas Critique forum and/or IRC chatrooms before asking for draft feedback.

Please first go to the Ideas forum or the chat, give a quick summary (for the Ideas forum, please follow the instructions in the required reading thread) of the concept you want to write up (don't link the draft unless someone requests it), and reviewers can help you make sure that your core idea is something that will be successful with the community audience.

During the conceptualization stage, reviewers can also help by letting you know if something similar already exists on the site, and/or telling you if there are any cliches/pitfalls/other typical downvote reasons to be careful of with your particular idea. These issues are more effectively addressed earlier on in the writing process.

If you have already received the requisite greenlights, please note from whom and where you received them. If you would like to receive draft critique without going through the greenlighting process, please use the IRC chatrooms to request reviews.

item.content:encoded:

Item #: SCP-XXXX

Object Class: Euclid

Special Containment Procedures:SCP-XXXX must be contained in a 10m x 10m reinforced concrete and steel chamber, the cell must be shined with standard light bulbs at all times and spotlights in the outer cell to prevent containment breach. If a light bulb is broken, three D-class personnel (no more, no less) must enter the cell with the cell doors closed behind them. One D-class must hold a flashlight towards SCP-XXXX while the other two D-class personnel can safely repair the light bulb.

Description: SCP-XXXX appears to be an old broken statue that was dated back to the mid-7th century BCE with an unknown origin, the object has a missing left elbow, the right arm seems to be intact, and holds a broken hilt. The object's face seems to be broken as well the face is missing a nose and a right ear. It stands over 7 feet and SCP-XXXX has a thick baseplate underneath that is measured to be 11 centimeters thick and has a chiseled title called "A Stone Heart", its weight was measured to be over 700 kilograms. SCP-XXXX have signs that tools were used to make SCP-XXXX, SCP-XXXX was chiseled from black andesite.

SCP-XXXX is hostile towards any human victims, SCP-XXXX cannot move when light touches the object, depending on its brightness. When light is removed from SCP-XXXX, the object anomalously moves towards the nearest subject, its speed depends on how dark the environment or containment it is in. Personnel reported noises of chiseling rocks created by SCP-XXXX when it moves its torso, head, or arms. When SCP-XXXX is close to its victim, SCP-XXXX will strike the victim's head with either its arm or its broken hilt with great force and speed. Testings on SCP-XXXX's movements were approved.

Testing 12 lumen (Candle light) - 7/██/██

Subject: D-32794

Procedure: D-class personnel was instructed to stand in a corner, the light in the containment changed to 12 lumens equivalent to wax candlelight.

Results: SCP-XXXX moves towards D-32794 slowly, at about 1kmph. D-32794 walks backward as she locks eye contact with SCP-XXXX movements.

Analysis: This was an interesting SCP, its movement depends highly on the light.

Testing 1 lumen (Moonlight) - 7/██/██

Subject: D-32794

Procedure: D-class personnel was instructed to stand in a corner as last time, the light in the containment changes to 1-lumen equivalent to moonlight.

Results: SCP-XXXX moves towards D-32794 with unbelievable speeds, SCP-XXXX kills D-32794 with the broken hilt.

Analysis: The speeds were calculated to be 70kmph after testing.

Testing (Complete Darkness) - █/██/██

Subject: D-23932

Procedure: D-class personnel were instructed to stand in a corner same as the last two tests, the containment's light turns off.

Results: As the lights turned off, the sound of a skull-cracking was heard in the SCP-XXXX containment cell. D-23932 was instantly killed after approximately 2 seconds when the lights turned off.

Analysis: Not only SCP-XXXX proved itself dangerous, but also unpredictable in its nature. Thus it's SCP-XXXX has classed into a Euclid class.
